item.title: [Sports Science 101 #15] Your Personal Exercise Prescription — and Everything This Semester Taught Us
item.body:
> Exercise works best when it's dosed like medicine — the FITT principle tells you how much, how hard, and how often, and it ties together everything we've covered this semester.

## Today's Concept

When a doctor prescribes medication, the label never just says "take some pills." It specifies the dose, the schedule, and the type. Exercise science treats physical activity the same way, using a framework called **exercise prescription**. The most common version is the **FITT principle**:

- **F**requency — how many days per week
- **I**ntensity — how hard (light, moderate, vigorous)
- **T**ime — how long each session lasts
- **T**ype — what kind of activity (aerobic, strength, flexibility, balance)

For most healthy adults, U.S. public health guidelines recommend at least **150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity per week** (or 75 minutes of vigorous activity), plus **muscle-strengthening work on 2 or more days**. How do you know your intensity without a lab? Use the **talk test**: at moderate intensity you can hold a conversation but couldn't sing; at vigorous intensity you can only get out a few words at a time.

Two more rules make a prescription actually work. **Progressive overload** means your body only adapts when you gradually ask a little more of it — slightly longer walks, slightly heavier weights. **Reversibility** is the flip side: stop training, and gains fade within weeks. Fitness is rented, not owned.

And this is where the whole semester comes together. Your muscles adapt because of the fiber types and energy systems we covered early on. Your heart and lungs improve through the same VO2 max mechanisms from our endurance lecture. Skill practice works through motor learning, food choices matter because of sports nutrition, and rest days matter because recovery and sleep are when adaptation actually happens. Even our doping lecture fits: shortcuts that skip the adaptation process carry real costs. An exercise prescription is simply all of that science, written down for one person — you.

## In Everyday Life

Meet Sarah, an accountant in Columbus, Ohio, who spends nine hours a day at a desk. She doesn't need a $200/month boutique gym. Her prescription might look like this: a brisk 30-minute walk through her neighborhood five days a week (that's her 150 minutes — moderate, by the talk test, because she can chat on the phone but not sing along to the radio), plus two short strength sessions at a $10/month budget gym or with a pair of dumbbells at home. After a month, overload kicks in: she walks a hillier route or adds five pounds to her goblet squat. If she takes two weeks off at Thanksgiving, reversibility means the first week back should be easier than where she left off — not a punishment workout. Nothing exotic, fully doable, and grounded in every principle this series covered.

## 3-Line Recap

1. Exercise prescription doses activity like medicine using FITT: Frequency, Intensity, Time, and Type.
2. The baseline for adults is 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity weekly plus strength training on 2+ days, with intensity checked by the talk test.
3. Progress comes from gradual overload, fades with inactivity (reversibility), and rests on everything this semester covered — energy systems, adaptation, nutrition, and recovery.

## ✅ Self-Quiz

1. In the FITT principle, what does the "I" stand for?
   (a) Interval  (b) Intensity  (c) Injury prevention  (d) Isolation
2. True or False: Under current U.S. guidelines, your weekly 150 minutes of moderate activity can be accumulated in short bouts — even a few minutes at a time count.
3. True or False: Once you've built fitness, the gains are permanent even if you stop exercising.

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Exercise prescription** — a structured plan specifying how often, how hard, how long, and what kind of exercise a person should do.
- **FITT principle** — the four adjustable dials of any exercise plan: Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type.
- **Talk test** — a practical intensity gauge: moderate means you can talk but not sing; vigorous means only a few words at a time.
- **Progressive overload** — gradually increasing demands on the body so it keeps adapting.
- **Reversibility** — the principle that fitness gains decline when training stops.

---

*Answers: 1. (b) — Intensity, or how hard you work, checked easily with the talk test. 2. True — the 2018 U.S. Physical Activity Guidelines removed the old 10-minute minimum, so all movement counts toward your weekly total. 3. False — that's reversibility; gains begin to fade within weeks of stopping, which is why consistency beats intensity.*
